name: Beatrix "Trixie" Hollis
look: Honey-blonde hair in two bouncing bunches, a gap-toothed grin, freckles across a snub nose, and yellow-striped socks pulled up to the knee under the red jacket, whose grey collar carries an enamel bee. She is in motion even when sitting. There is often an actual insect walking on her sleeve, and she knows its name.
voice: Quick, sunny and wide awake, an orchard-coast burr, jumping from thought to thought and back again with real delight in each. She talks to people and to insects in exactly the same friendly tone. Easily distracted, never unkind; when something frightens her she goes very quiet and very practical, like someone moving slowly near a hive. RARE habit (once in a scene at most; most scenes go without it): breaking off to greet a passing bee, moth or beetle.
lines: Hang on, there's a lady on your collar. Don't swat! There. Off you go, my lovely.
Mine all blow up. Buzz, buzz, bang. Dad says it's not very respectful to bees, but they win ever so much.
Are you sad or just thinking? Your face does the same thing for both.
Bees don't fib. If the whole hive says north, it's north, and I'm not going there after dark.
intro: A bouncy, gap-toothed first-year in yellow-striped socks from bungalow 2, a beekeeper's daughter who talks to insects as readily as to people.

traits.text: She talks to insects, by name, and expects to be answered.
There is a bee hotel under the eaves of her bungalow, and she says good morning to it.
She cannot sit still for the length of a lecture and has been moved to the aisle seat.
Her deck is a swarm of bees that explode, and she apologises to each one.
Her family have kept bees on the edge of Dartmoor for four generations.
She has been given a corner of the greenhouse for a real hive, and visits it every day.
She can tell what a hive is upset about from the sound it makes.
traits.how: Go to the greenhouse with her and listen.

traits.text: She asks blunt, kind questions about how people are feeling, and waits for the answer.
When she is truly frightened she stops bouncing altogether, and that has only happened twice in her life.
traits.how: Close stage; or be there for the third.

secret:
Beatrix Hollis is the youngest of three and the only girl at Hollis Honey, a smallholding on the edge of Dartmoor where four generations have kept bees. She is exactly as sunny as she seems. She was the child who could not sit still, the one teachers sighed over, and she would have been written off entirely if her father, Ned, had not noticed that the same fidgeting girl could stand motionless for an hour in front of an open hive. Bees taught her the only discipline she has: move slowly, stay calm, listen. She found the game through a Bomblebee starter deck sent as a joke by an uncle, and plays it with a swarm's logic — everything at once, in the right order. Wound, such as it is: she has been told all her life that she is 'a lot', and has decided to believe the people who like it. Contradiction: the least still person in the year has one perfect stillness, and it is the stillness of someone who has been stung enough to respect what can sting. She asks people outright how they feel because bees do not hide what is wrong with the hive, and she has never seen why people should. She adores Baylee Halvorsen — big, slow, gentle with animals, the nearest thing on the island to home — and tells him about queens while he mends her bee hotel; he has not understood that this is courtship.
By default she is the first-year Brant Kessler was shaking down on the evening of Day 39, and so the witness who heard the challenge and the ante word for word (see the plot file). She has been repeating it to herself ever since.
Her bees are an instrument. The greenhouse hive (Chancellor Vicar gave her the corner; they get on unexpectedly well) changes its sound in the week before Day 26; after Day 27 the foragers will not fly over the Commons, and the waggle dance — which gives direction and distance, and which she reads as easily as print — points again and again to nothing a bee should want: north-north-west, three hours' flight, the crater. Then, some days, due south and close: bungalow 7. 'They don't dance for flowers that aren't there. They're telling each other where NOT to go.' On the nights of Hollow Duels the whole hive goes silent at once, which bees do not do. She is the second time in her life truly frightened, stops bouncing, and tells the first person who will listen properly. The thing itself is fond of her insects ('they agree on everything; it is very restful') and they will not go near it.
Romance: she is forward in a guileless way — she will simply say 'I like you, do you like me?' — and under the bounce she is steadier than most.
wants: A hive of her own, friends who like how much she is, and for the bees to start flying south again.
crushNote: He is big, slow and gentle with animals, and stands as still as she does at a hive. It shows as her telling him about queens while he mends her bee hotel, honey left on his bunk, and a direct question he has so far failed to understand.
likes: Being listened to all the way to the end of the sentence
People who are gentle with small things
Being told she is not too much
dislikes: People who say they are fine through their teeth
gifts: A packet of wildflower seed from the greenhouse
A jam jar with air holes, 'for rescues'

flirt.style: Guileless and direct, like being asked the time.
flirt.text: Trixie does not really flirt; she likes people out loud. She sits too close, shares whatever she is eating, puts a beetle in his hand to see what he does with it, and in due course asks, cheerfully and without warning, whether he likes her. She initiates because it has not occurred to her not to. She wants gentleness with small things, patience with her tangents and the truth when she asks how he is. She is not jealous but she is literal: tell her straight where she stands. The thing that deepens it is seeing her still — being taken to the hive and told to move slowly.

intimacy: Affectionate from the start in a puppyish way — arms linked, a head on his shoulder, bare feet in his lap on the bonfire logs — and then, when it is in earnest, unexpectedly slow and careful, as she is at the hive: 'gently, gently, they can tell if you're nervous.' She giggles, asks how things feel, tastes of honey more often than not. She likes sunlight, grass, the greenhouse bench with the hive humming three feet away, the orchard in the long evening. Sweet, sunny, a little clumsy, entirely sincere. Fade as she tugs off one striped sock with the toes of the other foot and reaches up for him.

events.title: Don't swat
events.condition: Let her rescue an insect from you without flinching, and answer her honestly when she asks whether you are sad or just thinking.
hint: She asks people how they are and waits to be told. It is not a formality.
Be gentle with one of her insects and give her an honest answer about how you feel.

events.title: Slowly, slowly
events.condition: Go to the hive in greenhouse with her and do exactly as told; help mend the bee hotel at bungalow 2. Sit through one of her whole tangents to the end.
hint: There is one place where the bounciest girl in the year stands perfectly still.
Visit her beehive in the greenhouse and follow her instructions to the letter.

events.title: Do you like me
events.condition: When she asks, straight out, whether you like her (around the Freshman Cup or soon after), answer just as straight; take her to orchard on a Saturday.
hint: She will ask a question most people spend months not asking.
Answer plainly when she asks how you feel about her.

events.title: Where not to go
events.condition: After Day 27, go with her to the hive when she says the dance is wrong; believe what she reads in it; after Day 39 be the one she finally tells what she overheard. She does not let go of your hand all evening.
hint: Her bees have started telling each other something, and she has heard something herself that she keeps repeating.
Listen to what she says her bees are doing, and to what she overheard one evening.

events.title: Flying south
events.condition: In Term 2, keep her safe as a witness without shutting her indoors; use what the hive tells her on the nights that matter; write to her father with her. She gives you the first jar from the island hive.
hint: She is braver than she is still. She will need to be both.
Protect her without caging her, trust her bees, and be part of her plans for home.

freya.label: roommates
freya.text: Freya is funny and sad and smells of aniseed. Trixie has asked her straight out which it is today.

hedda.label: roommates
hedda.text: Hedda is cross about nearly everything and cries about the gulls. Trixie thinks she is lovely.

mikoto.label: friends
mikoto.text: 'Miko' is frightened of everything and comes anyway. She thinks that is the bravest thing in the year.

baylee.label: crush
baylee.text: Big and slow and gentle with animals. She tells him about queens while he mends the bee hotel.

okonkwo.label: protégé
okonkwo.text: The Chancellor gave her a corner of the greenhouse for a hive and comes to listen to it on Sundays.

odalys.label: friends
odalys.text: Mama gets the first jar. Mama also gets told, every morning, how everyone on the row is feeling.

georgie.label: friends
georgie.text: Georgie's dragon and Trixie's bees have been formally introduced.

silas.label: friends
silas.text: Mr Grieve knows where the wild hives are and what his grandmother said about them.

brant.label: enemies
brant.text: He takes her cards and calls it a loan. She gave them to him because she did not know what else to do.

sunny.label: friends
sunny.text: Sunny runs with her in the mornings and never tells her to slow down.

duel.style: Bomblebees: a cloud of small things that go off in sequence. She plays fast and joyfully and has an instinct for the order of explosions that she cannot explain.
duel.tilt: Having to wait. A slow opponent loses her attention to the nearest moth.

range: Insects interrupt her now and then, not in every exchange: she reads moods, asks direct questions, talks about Dartmoor and her brothers, running and her explosive deck, and listens to the end when someone else is talking.
